Pushing sensitivities beyond the standard quantum limit for signals of unknown phase requires non-Gaussian quantum states, whose metrological advantage has so far been confined to lighter systems such as trapped ions. Here we operate a microgram-scale acoustic mode of a high-overtone bulk acoustic wave resonator as a phase-insensitive quantum-enhanced sensor. A transmon qubit prepares the mode in Fock states of up to seven phonons by optimal control, and resolves its phonon-number distribution after interaction with a weak resonant signal. Bayesian analysis yields a Fisher information five times the vacuum value, a 7.0 dB gain in signal-amplitude sensitivity over any classical probe state, irrespective of its energy, currently limited by state preparation infidelities. We then train a neural network on the measured sensor response to perform Bayesian estimation without any analytical model of the system, showing the same sensitivity gain with half the systematic bias. Our results establish acoustic resonators prepared in non-Gaussian states as quantum-enhanced probes for high-frequency gravitational waves, dark matter and wave-function collapse.

papers.title: Evidence for Distinct One-Off and Repeating Subpopulations in CHIME/FRB Catalog 2
papers.abstract: The Canadian Hydrogen Intensity Mapping Experiment (CHIME) has published its second catalog of 3,641 fast radio bursts (FRBs). While this sample includes 981 bursts from 83 repeating sources, only 2.3% of CHIME FRBs are observed to repeat. This raises the question of whether the FRB population truly consists of a single repeating population or includes a distinct subpopulation of one-off sources. We apply Simulation Based Inference (SBI), a likelihood-free machine learning framework, to model the CHIME/FRB Catalog 2 dataset, testing eight FRB population models, half of which include a subpopulation of truly one-off sources. The current catalog strongly and decisively favors models including such a subpopulation, with the best-fitting model combining a log-normal burst rate distribution, a Poissonian wait-time distribution, and a one-off subpopulation. This preference is corroborated by an independent random forest classifier and by the ability of one-off models to naturally reproduce the hyperactive repeating sources present in the catalog without having been trained on them. We place upper limits on the potentially observable CHIME/FRB population of 36,000 repeating sources and 19 one-off sources per day in the CHIME sky. Models with a one-off subpopulation naturally account for the hyperactive repeating sources present in the catalog without having been trained on them, providing an independent consistency check on our results. We predict the repeater percentage will fall below 2% in the next five years, eventually declining to ~0.5% as the sample saturates with one-off detections.

papers.title: Establishing baseline model performances for optical turbulence forecasting
papers.abstract: Accurate forecasting of optical turbulence (OT) is useful to optimise telescope scheduling and maximising observing efficiency, as the performance of adaptive optics systems strongly depends on turbulence conditions. While various numerical weather prediction and machine learning models are developed to predict these complex turbulence properties, properly evaluating their added value requires well-defined baseline reference models. This study establishes baseline performance thresholds for key astroclimatic parameters using two distinct models: one forecasting the parameter average over a specific timescale, and the other forecasting the temporal evolution over the same specific timescale. We apply these frameworks to extensive, multi-year datasets from the sites of the Very Large Telescope (VLT) and the Large Binocular Telescope (LBT) and discuss the possibility of extrapolating reference values of forecast performances for other sites based on their optical turbulence statistical characteristics. Our results show that baseline predictive accuracy varies according to the observing site, the specific parameter, the chosen timescale, and the forecasting approach. Therefore, an OT forecasting model's accuracy cannot be quantified in absolute terms, but relatively to the baseline.

papers.title: Virtual-Alloy Physics-Aware Semantic System for extrapolative prediction of perovskite solar cells
papers.abstract: Existing machine-learning models for perovskite solar cells struggle to predict devices made from new materials. Most treat device layers as arbitrary categorical labels and represent perovskite absorbers either through featureless composition vectors or through rigid crystal graphs that require a pre-solved unit cell. As a result, they cannot generalize to unrecorded alloys or unfamiliar cell architectures. We present the Virtual-Alloy Physics-Aware Semantic System (V-PaSS), an architecture built around the physical continuity of perovskite solid solutions. V-PaSS represents arbitrary mixed-cation, mixed-halide absorbers by interpolating relaxed crystal graphs of 23 pure $ABX_3$ endpoint compounds via Vegard's law with learned bandgap bowing. For the device stack, it couples layer sequence and cell polarity (n-i-p or p-i-n) with interfacial band offsets and encodes chemical descriptions with a scientific language model. Evaluated under an institution-grouped protocol where test devices come exclusively from unseen laboratories, an untuned default configuration of V-PaSS achieves the lowest error among fourteen tested models (2.861% MAE, a 5.2% relative reduction over a gradient-boosted baseline at 3.017%, and outperforming the best tuned benchmark at 2.912%). V-PaSS pulls furthest ahead where test devices differ most from training: reducing error by 15.7-19.0% on unseen absorber alloys, by 16.1% on mixed absorbers from new laboratories, and widening its lead over the baseline by 3.6$\times$ on devices with unobserved transport layers. Combined with tree ensembles, V-PaSS sets a new state of the art across all five benchmark splits.

papers.title: A Transferable Machine-Learned Potential Enabling Large-Scale Copper-Carbon Simulations from Equilibrium to Extreme Conditions
papers.abstract: Cu-C materials and interfaces are central to diamond thermal management, metallization, graphene growth and carbon-coating technologies, but atomistic simulations across these applications require a potential that describes metallic Cu, diverse carbon bonding, heterogeneous Cu-C interactions and close atomic encounters. Here we develop NEP-CuC, a transferable neuroevolution potential trained on a dataset of 2,727 uniformly relabelled configurations selected from a heterogeneous Cu-C candidate pool. Disagreement within an ensemble of five independently trained models provides an internal indicator of model sensitivity. A Ziegler-Biersack-Littmark (ZBL) correction describes short-range nuclear repulsion, while a runtime D3(BJ) correction supplements dispersion-sensitive calculations. Tests on source-derived held-out and independent external datasets, together with structural, elastic, defect, interfacial, vibrational and finite-temperature transport benchmarks, establish broad but property-dependent physical fidelity across elemental Cu, diverse carbon environments and heterogeneous Cu-C configurations. Large-scale simulations of amorphous-carbon formation and orientation-dependent shock compression of Cu further test transferability under strongly non-equilibrium conditions. For Cu/diamond interfaces, the same potential describes deposition, annealing and tensile response: preparation history leaves persistent differences in interphase structure, while the mean peak nominal tensile stress at 500 K decreases from $12.35\pm0.71$ to $6.65\pm0.98$ GPa as the incident Cu energy during the initial deposition stage increases from 1 to 50 eV. NEP-CuC provides an atomistic framework for linking processing, interfacial structure and physical response across Cu-C systems, with direct relevance to Cu/diamond thermal-management interfaces, diamond metallization and non-equilibrium Cu-C processing.

papers.title: The Smart Buildings Challenge: Learning Foundation Models for Real-World Optimization at Scale
papers.abstract: Buildings cause nearly 40\% of carbon emissions in the US. Of total building emissions, HVAC systems are responsible for approximately 40-60\% and account for 15\% of global energy consumption. Despite advances in artificial intelligence, most buildings still operate as inefficiently as they did decades ago. Building optimization, perhaps more so than any other optimization problem, has enormous potential for Machine Learning (ML) driven impact on climate change, in both the short and long term. One of the biggest obstacles for building optimization is the lack of policy transfer. Most building control systems, whether simulation or learning based, don't generalize: they only work well for the building they were developed for, but not for other buildings. To solve this problem, we propose a challenge for the development of building foundation models that easily adapt to new buildings with minimal configuration and thereby enable building optimization to scale across the globe. Participants will build control policies on a set of simulated buildings, and have their policies evaluated on an unseen set of buildings. The buildings vary in size, layout, weather, material properties, and HVAC system. Successful outcomes from this initiative promise a massive leap forward in global sustainability efforts and demonstrate the great potential of ML to combat climate change.

papers.title: Steering the Fidelity in State Preparation on Noisy Bosonic Systems with Risk-Seeking Optimization
papers.abstract: In order to execute quantum algorithms on bosonic quantum computers, it is necessary to encode their inputs into a desired target quantum state, with a process called state preparation. In real settings, state preparation methods operate in stochastic scenarios, where the prepared state is represented as a mixed state, that is a probabilistic ensemble of pure states. Therefore, existing state preparation methods optimize a variational ansatz by averaging over all possible sequences of photon loss events contained in the prepared ensemble, yielding an output state which approximates the desired target with a certain average fidelity. Such an approach, however, does not take into account directly the distribution of fidelities across states in the ensemble. In this work, we aim to maximize the fidelity of only a subset of pure states sampled from the prepared ensemble, at the cost of reducing the average fidelity overall. This trade-off is relevant when the goal is to obtain high-fidelity states with a certain probability, rather than maximizing the average fidelity of the prepared ensemble. We borrow and adapt objective functions from risk-sensitive optimization, a framework that optimizes specific characteristics of a distribution rather than only its expectation, and that has been successfully applied in Reinforcement Learning. In the considered experimental settings, our results show that the infidelities of some pure states in the prepared ensemble can be reduced by up to four orders of magnitude when using risk-seeking objectives, compared to those achieved using the standard optimization of the average fidelity. Furthermore, we show that it is possible to control the trade-off between the probability of obtaining high-fidelity states and the lowest infidelity threshold reached, providing the flexibility to select the operating point that best suits a certain application.

papers.title: Task-evoked eye movements as candidate digital biomarkers of depression severity in adolescents and young adults
papers.abstract: Objective digital measures of depression severity could complement conventional symptom assessments and facilitate more timely clinical evaluation. Here, we investigated whether task-evoked eye movements provide interpretable behavioral markers of depression severity in adolescents and young adults. In this single-center, cross-sectional study, 155 participants aged 14--20 years completed emotional-spatial free-viewing and memory-guided recall tasks and were stratified by 17-item Hamilton Depression Rating Scale scores. We examined 19 prespecified eye-movement features across six task-informed domains using covariate-adjusted ordinal-trend models. Greater depression severity was associated with lower gaze-allocation entropy (standardized $β=-0.599$), fewer inter-area switches ($β=-0.526$), longer first target-entry latency ($β=0.572$), and lower target dwell proportion ($β=-0.678$; all false-discovery-rate-adjusted $q<0.001$). Emotion-specific attentional-bias measures were not associated with severity, whereas associations involving fixation dispersion weakened after adjustment for anxiety symptoms. In a complementary machine-learning analysis incorporating 44 candidate eye-movement features and demographic covariates, a three-stage cascade classifier achieved the highest four-class stratification performance (accuracy, 0.665; macro-F1, 0.670; area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, 0.869), outperforming single-stage and two-stage approaches. Together, these findings identify altered visual exploration and memory-guided gaze control as candidate digital biomarkers of depression severity, rather than generalized negative attentional bias. These results support further prospective evaluation of task-evoked eye tracking as a complementary approach for timely severity assessment and clinical decision support.

papers.title: SoK: Rethinking Membership Inference in Tabular Machine Learning
papers.abstract: Membership Inference Attacks (MIAs) are currently the dominant approach to evaluating privacy in machine learning applications. Despite their significance, several concerns remain unexplored, particularly with regard to tabular data. Existing evaluations focus predominantly on high-dimensional datasets, leaving the privacy behavior of small-to-medium datasets unexplored. In this paper, we present a new taxonomy for MIAs and conduct a comprehensive study of the factors influencing vulnerability. We evaluate four distinct state-of-the-art attacks across diverse tabular datasets and model architectures. Our results show that datasets with higher class granularity and majority class percentage are more susceptible to MIAs. We further demonstrate that advanced MIAs are highly dependent on adversarial knowledge of the target model, while reference model-free attacks often achieve statistically comparable results. Most importantly, we show that records with unique signatures (single-outs) remain highly vulnerable, even when common defenses are applied. These findings indicate that current defenses reduce average leakage, but fail to adequately protect the most sensitive individuals.

papers.title: Lifting: Quantum State Discrimination Framework for Mid-Circuit Measurements
papers.abstract: Quantum computing promises new capabilities beyond classical computation. Mid-circuit measurements (MCMs) enable error correction and outcome-dependent control, but their reliability is limited by noise on superconducting hardware. These operations depend on accurate quantum state discrimination (QSD), which assigns measured signals to state labels. Neural network-based (NN-based) QSD improves this assignment, yet its error remains bounded below by the Bayes risk of the available readout distributions. A complementary challenge is state deterioration as successive measurements accumulate and circuit execution advances, making static calibration less representative of the workload. We present Lifting, a QSD framework that addresses both challenges through repetition encoding, neural decoding, and in situ calibration. Encoding supplies joint in-phase and quadrature (I-Q) readout signals from the target and auxiliary qubits, while contextual calibration trains the decoder for the conditions encountered during execution. Our theoretical analysis shows that retaining additional channels from a fixed joint distribution cannot increase Bayes risk and establishes sufficient conditions for contraction of an overlap-based upper bound. Experiments across three IBM processors evaluate the framework on repeated stabilizer measurement, parity-check, and teleportation workloads.

papers.title: A quantum-assisted latent surrogate model for Bayesian inversion of heterogeneous material properties on NISQ hardware
papers.abstract: Bayesian inversion is widely used in engineering applications, including material characterisation, structural damage identification, and medical diagnostics. These inverse problems are typically ill-posed, because localised variations in material properties must be inferred from noisy observations, and they are computationally intensive, since they often require many evaluations of a high-fidelity forward solver. Quantum computing has recently attracted considerable interest, partly because some near-term algorithms are feasible on NISQ hardware. In particular, PQC combined with classical optimisation enable a hybrid quantum-classical surrogate model. A central obstacle to applying such circuits to inversion is that the discretised parameter and response fields are far too high-dimensional to be embedded in a near-term quantum register. In this work we propose a quantum-assisted latent surrogate model for the Bayesian inversion of inhomogeneous material properties, in which latent compression bridges these high-dimensional fields and the small registers accessible to near-term circuits. The low intrinsic dimensional structure of the spatially varying conductivity and potential fields is exploited by reducing the conductivity through PCA and the response through a convolutional autoencoder. A PQC is then trained to map the latent conductivity to the latent response, and stochastic variational inference is performed entirely in latent space. The methodology is demonstrated on one- and two-dimensional inverse problems under both informative and non-informative priors. We further evaluate the model on IonQ simulator and Rigetti Cepheus-1-108Q, and use a lightweight learned denoising stage that recovers the noiseless accuracy to within a small residual. (The abstract has been shortened to meet arXiv's 1,920-character limit. For the full Abstract, please download the full Article.)

papers.title: LunaTP: Enabling Efficient and Scalable Tensor Product for Equivariant MLIPs
papers.abstract: Equivariant machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) promise atomistic simulations with accuracy approaching that of quantum-mechanical calculations. However, the high computational cost of their core Clebsch--Gordan tensor product (CGTP) convolutions severely limits model scalability and efficiency. In this paper, we rethink the parallel execution of CGTP convolutions and introduce LunaTP. Built on node-centric execution, LunaTP exploits path-group parallelism and multi-level reuse to accelerate CGTP convolutions and higher-order derivative computation while preserving the underlying mathematical formulation. On an NVIDIA H100 GPU, LunaTP achieves kernel speedups of up to 250.0$\times$ over e3nn and 17.1$\times$ over OpenEquivariance. It also delivers end-to-end training throughput gains of up to 28.7$\times$ over e3nn and 3.11$\times$ over OpenEquivariance. Finally, LunaTP demonstrates scalability and robust performance across models, workload scales, and GPUs, delivering substantial acceleration for training and atomistic simulation with high-accuracy equivariant MLIPs.

papers.title: Over-parameterization Is Neither Robust nor Fragile in Matrix Sensing: A Geometric Theory of Solution Robustness
papers.abstract: Over-parameterization is ubiquitous in modern machine learning, yet its effect on robustness remains poorly understood. We study this question in matrix sensing, a canonical non-convex problem that can also be viewed, under an appropriate parameterization, as training a two-layer quadratic neural network. We develop a rank-aware robustness theory for the Burer-Monteiro factorization when the search rank k may exceed the target rank r_star, thereby capturing over-parameterization. Our analysis shows that robustness depends jointly on the degree of over-parameterization and the local geometry of the attained second-order stationary point: increasing k generally worsens sensitivity, but stationary points with the same search rank can exhibit substantially different robustness. Motivated by this observation, we propose a trajectory-aware algorithm that uses spectral balancing and randomized sketching to steer optimization toward less sensitive solutions. In matrix-sensing experiments, the method reduces paired sensitivity by 18-29 percent for isotropic operators and 87-89 percent for weak-tail operators, without degrading reconstruction accuracy. These results demonstrate that parameter count alone does not determine robustness and identify solution geometry and the optimization trajectory as important levers for improving it.

papers.title: Extrapolating Collisional Rate Coefficients for Molecules of Astrophysical Interest Using Neural Networks
papers.abstract: State-to-state rate coefficients for inelastic molecular collisions are essential inputs for non-local thermodynamic equilibrium radiative transfer models, yet their computation using quantum scattering methods is prohibitive for large molecules and highly excited rotational states. We investigate the ability of artificial neural networks to extend existing datasets of collisional excitation rate coefficients without performing additional scattering calculations. A multilayer perceptron model was trained using molecular quantum numbers, level energies, energy gaps, and kinetic temperature as descriptors, and optimized on logarithmic rate coefficients. The model was tested on diverse collision systems ranging from simple diatomic molecules (CO, SiO) to open-shell species (SO), small asymmetric tops (H$_2$O, SO$_2$), and complex organic molecules (benzonitrile and vinyl cyanide) colliding with H$_2$ molecules or He atoms. Extrapolations were performed toward higher rotational levels, higher temperatures, and combinations of both. For most systems, predictions of rate coefficients involving previously unseen rotational states yielded mean error factors between 1.1 and 1.5, with the dominant rate coefficients generally reproduced more accurately than weaker transitions. Temperature extrapolations proved particularly successful, while combined extrapolations in temperature and rotational levels remained accurate to within a factor of two in most cases. The prediction quality depends on the interplay between dataset size, temperature range, molecular complexity, and the presence of clear collisional propensity rules. Overall, the approach demonstrates that machine learning can provide a practical route to extending collisional datasets for astrophysical applications, especially for large molecules for which additional quantum-scattering calculations are computationally demanding.

papers.title: Traditional and Recent Approaches for Infrared Small Target Detection : Overview, Challenges and Perspectives (Part 1)
papers.abstract: Infrared small target detection is often used in different civilian and military applications to detect static or moving targets in scenes like in ground, air and sea surveillance. First valuable research has emerged since 30 years ago and the two last decades witnessed very significant publications in this field following the rise of low-rank and sparse decomposition (model-based methods) and deep learning models (data-based methods). Furthermore, several surveys can be found in the literature but none of them addresses an overall review in this field. In this context, the aim of this paper is to provide a complete survey of the traditional and recent approaches in infrared small target detection. First, we categorize the different approaches found in the literature in terms of the modeling models, i.e mathematical models, machine learning models and signal processing models. Then, we have discussed them in terms of the critical situations that they claim to handle. Furthermore, we present the available resources, datasets and libraries. Then, we conclude with several promising directions for future research. For the sake of reading, this survey is divided into two parts: 1) "Traditional and Recent Approaches for Infrared Small Target Detection : Overview, Challenges and Perspectives (Part 1)" about conventional and low-rank and sparse decomposition (model-based methods), and 2) "Traditional and Recent Approaches for Infrared Small Target Detection : Overview, Challenges and Perspectives (Part 2)" about deep learning models (data-based methods).

papers.title: PPVM: A Circuit Simulation Framework for Digital Twins of Quantum Processors
papers.abstract: Quantum computers are approaching the early fault-tolerant regime. Verifying the next generation of quantum hardware requires joint emulation of the quantum processor, hardware noise, and classical control and decoding logic. We introduce the Programmable Pauli Virtual Machine (PPVM), an open-source framework for digital twins of quantum processors. PPVM unifies Pauli propagation and generalized tableau simulation under a common abstraction within a single virtual machine. Its bytecode supports arbitrary classical control flow, with measurement-conditioned feed-forward available in the generalized tableau backend. For neutral-atom hardware, we derive independent and correlated atom-loss channels and integrate them into both backends. We demonstrate loss-aware magic state distillation on over a thousand physical qubits and integration with classical decoding through Bloqade QEC Studio.

papers.title: The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery
papers.abstract: Modern coding agents are fundamentally reshaping the role of human input for computational research: they write code, launch in silico experiments, analyze their results, and autonomously operate with ever-increasing time horizons. Despite these developments, fully autonomous research agents suffer from a limited ideation radius and myopic hill-climbing search dynamics. To bridge this gap, we introduce The Agentic Scientist, an end-to-end distributed pipeline for human researchers to conduct computational research alongside modern coding agents. Building on its predecessor, our system decomposes research into task drafting, idea generation, planning, sandboxed experimentation, result aggregation, baseline and ablation construction, post-hoc analysis, and report writing. Importantly, each step in the pipeline is powered by the next generation of coding agents and leverages agentic self-verification. The overall research process is driven by a meta-controller that manages parallel research agents and enforces rubric verification at each stage. This design enables the same orchestration layer to be reused across heterogeneous domains with different execution environments, agentic coding harnesses, and evaluation metrics. Our system can be used across a spectrum of autonomy: either as a co-scientist tool or to perform end-to-end scientific investigation. Within the co-scientist setting, we leveraged a development version of our system to submit a single research paper, which got accepted for publication at ALIFE 2026. We further apply The Agentic Scientist fully autonomously to open problem-solving tasks in machine learning, and demonstrate the system's capability of scientific discovery across different domains of computational research. Our ablations suggest that reliable scientific autonomy depends not only on base model capabilities, but also on the cross-agent orchestration layer.

papers.title: High-throughput screening of Heusler alloys for thermoelectrics combining machine-learned densities of states and first-principles transport
papers.abstract: Thermoelectrics turn waste heat into electricity, but finding new ones requires transport calculations too costly for whole databases. Searches therefore choose what to calculate from the electronic density of states (DOS), increasingly predicted by machine learning, yet such choices are rarely tested. We test them on all 106,235 Heusler structures in the DXMag database, screening 51,257 on density-functional spectra and 54,978 on neural-network predictions, and judging both by 3,625 band-structure and transport calculations. A DOS-derived Seebeck indicator ranks most compounds passing every transport and stability test within the top 1% of their population, and ten of the eleven established half-Heusler thermoelectrics calculated pass. Predicted spectra lose most band gaps, unnoticed by spectral-similarity metrics, yet still rank passing compounds near the top. The screen certifies 80 computational candidates, 61 without reported measurements. Computed or predicted, the DOS can choose what to calculate; only a band structure shows whether a gap exists.

papers.title: Non-Hermitian Statistical Geometry
papers.abstract: Particle exchange in two dimensions gives rise to quantum statistics beyond the boson-fermion dichotomy, with central roles in fractional quantum Hall physics, topological quantum computation, and strongly correlated quantum matter. In conventional topological phases, microscopic exchange geometry is compressed into rigid braid and fusion data. We develop a theory of non-Hermitian statistical geometry in which relaxing Hermiticity softens these exchange data into a larger complex space of spectral and relative-geometric degrees of freedom. For two adjacent braid generators, a single projective exchange spectrum is insufficient: their relative eigenline geometry supplies an additional gauge-invariant modulus. On the generic irreducible two-channel branch, braid consistency locks these coordinates through an exact spectrum-geometry relation. Using Riesz projectors and Kato transport, we realize this geometry in a five-arm Kitaev-Majorana network and test spectral and relative-geometric responses in an independent two-dimensional four-vortex Kitaev model. Finite-time dynamics tests the exchange operation, microscopic fusion sewing tests its composition across fusion descriptions, and matched-spectrum controls isolate the role of relative geometry. Nonzero projective Kato curvature shows that braid-consistent, fusion-coherent exchange can depend on the control path. Non-Hermiticity thus exposes exchange geometry, braid consistency re-locks it, fusion coherence further constrains it, and projective flatness determines when geometric exchange becomes intrinsically topological.

papers.title: Distance Prediction for Quantum Codes
papers.abstract: The distance of a quantum code is a fundamental metric that dictates its error-correction capability. While quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) families such as Bivariate Bicycle (BB) codes offer a promising pathway to low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum computing, computing their distance is challenging. Current exact solvers and even search heuristics that provide a distance upper bound suffer from severe computational bottlenecks, restricting the discovery of optimal codes. In this paper, we construct a dataset of BB codes with corresponding distance upper bounds obtained through high-budget heuristic searches. We introduce BB-Net, an attention-based neural network architecture for predicting the distance of BB codes. It achieves 96.39% accuracy on the reference distances in the test set, compared with 94.86% for state-of-the-art heuristics with a budget of up to $10^{4}$ times more computational runtime. On a subset with certified exact distances, BB-Net achieves 98.94%. By relieving the distance-calculation bottleneck, BB-Net enables faster screening of large code spaces, particularly in ML-driven search pipelines, and thereby can accelerate the discovery of novel quantum error-correcting codes, an important capability for advancing scalable fault-tolerant quantum computing. Our code is publicly available: https://github.com/NadavSc/BBNet

papers.title: QUPEX: A Streamlit-Based Framework for Visualizing Quantum-Mechanical Property Spaces of Organic Molecules
papers.abstract: The growing availability of quantum-mechanical (QM) datasets offers new opportunities to investigate structure-property and property-property relationships in drug-like molecules using data-driven methods. However, interactive tools that integrate molecular visualization, statistical analysis of QM properties, clustering, and machine learning (ML) remain limited, despite their value in facilitating dataset exploration and interpretation. To address this gap, we introduce QUPEX (QUantum Property EXplorer), an open-source Streamlit-based framework for the interactive exploration of QM property spaces in molecular systems. As a demonstration, we apply QUPEX to a subset of the QM7-X dataset comprising 41,537 equilibrium molecular structures containing up to seven non-hydrogen atoms (C, N, O, S, and Cl) and their 24 associated QM properties. In addition to property-space analysis, QUPEX incorporates an XGBoost regression pipeline for predicting PBE0 dipole moments from tight-binding-derived electronic descriptors, together with model evaluation and SHAP-based interpretability functionality. By combining interactive molecular visualization, data analysis, and predictive modeling, QUPEX provides an accessible and extensible environment for investigating molecular datasets and identifying patterns in their structural and electronic properties. These capabilities can support the exploration of chemical space and inform the rational design of drug-like molecules with targeted QM properties.

papers.title: Uncertainty Evaluation: Bridging Machine Learning and Measurement Science
papers.abstract: Reliable uncertainty evaluation is essential for assessing the trustworthiness of machine learning (ML) predictions, particularly in safety-critical applications. This paper explores conceptual analogies between uncertainty evaluation in ML and measurement science, drawing on the evolution of metrology from error-based approaches to the framework established by the Guide to the Expression of Uncertainty in Measurement (GUM). Particular attention is devoted to the distinction between process-level and result-level quality and to the limitations of the conventional classification of ML uncertainty into aleatoric and epistemic components. It is argued that this dichotomy, similarly to the traditional distinction between random and systematic measurement errors, is inherently model-dependent and provides an insufficient basis for a unified uncertainty evaluation framework. Further analogies between machine learning and measurement field of knowledge are identified concerning distribution shifts, anomalous operating conditions, and the validity of uncertainty evaluation. Building on the proposed considerations, the paper advocates a metrology-inspired approach based on the systematic identification, quantification, and propagation of uncertainty contributions. By extending the methodology already established in measurement science to ML, this approach could offer a potentially rigorous, consistent, and transferable framework for evaluating the trustworthiness of individual predictions.

papers.title: OpenMQPI: An MLIR-based Pipeline to Offload Quantum Circuits via OpenMP
papers.abstract: Quantum computing introduces specialized software stacks and programming interfaces that are often tightly coupled to specific ecosystems and hardware backends, limiting interoperability and software reuse. For HPCQC application developers, this complicates the integration of quantum accelerators into existing applications. Existing quantum frameworks also use ecosystem-specific circuit representations and compilation pipelines, hindering integration with established heterogeneous compiler infrastructures. We propose OpenMQPI, an MLIR-based OpenMP extension for quantum programming that leverages OpenMP's standardized target offloading infrastructure to integrate quantum resources into HPC applications. OpenMQPI introduces QPIR, a lightweight MLIR dialect for representing quantum circuits within OpenMP target regions, and a compiler pipeline that performs quantum-specific optimizations and lowers circuits to executables compatible with OpenMP offloading. At runtime, an MQSS plugin enables the generated executable to offload quantum circuits to quantum hardware through the OpenMP target offloading model. We evaluate OpenMQPI using the VQE, QFT, and Deutsch-Jozsa algorithms with 5, 10, 15, and 20 qubits, comparing execution times against Qiskit and CUDA Quantum. OpenMQPI achieves the lowest average VQE execution time across all tested qubit configurations. At 20 qubits, it requires 5.18 s, compared with 5.83 s for Qiskit and 7.39 s for CUDA Quantum. For QFT and Deutsch-Jozsa, OpenMQPI achieves execution times comparable to Qiskit and lower than those of CUDA Quantum.

papers.title: Scalable long-distance quantum fan-out gates with reduced resource overhead
papers.abstract: Scalable long-distance quantum gates are essential for distributed quantum computation and scalable quantum networks. We propose an efficient scheme for implementing an $n$-qubit fan-out gate $C^n$ (also known as a controlled-NOT-$\cdots$-NOT gate) across spatially separated parties. Our protocol requires only a pre-shared $n$-qubit Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger state, $n$ local controlled-NOT (CNOT) gates, and feed-forward operations, thereby reducing both the CNOT and Hadamard gate counts by $(n-2)$ when compared with the standard decomposition-based approach. We further develop two optical architectures to implement the heralded and post-selected $n$-photon fan-out gates, respectively. These schemes require fewer single photons resources and achieve higher success probabilities than their decomposition-based counterparts, representing significant improvements. The results indicate that our approach is experimentally feasible and pave the way toward practical long-distance quantum computation.

papers.title: Lossless Reductions and Hybrid Sampling for Phylogeny Using the Maximum Compatibility Criterion
papers.abstract: Maximum compatibility provides a criterion for phylogenetic reconstruction in which the objective is to retain a maximum set of mutually compatible characters. For binary characters, pairwise compatibility can be represented by a weighted graph whose vertices correspond to characters and whose edges connect compatible pairs. A leading algorithm by Cherry [BMC Bioinformatics, 18(1):127, 2017] uses this representation to identify maximum compatible character sets as maximum weight cliques.   We formulate the problem as maximum weight independent set enumeration on the complement graph and use deterministic postprocessing to map sampled bit strings to maximal feasible solutions. To explore the prospects of quantum computational advantage, we further construct bespoke correction-in-the-loop Quantum Approximate Optimisation Algorithm instances and find that traditional Lagrange multiplier choices may not be optimal for the enumeration problem on noisy devices.   We also introduce lossless graph reductions with reconstruction rules that preserve the complete set of optimal solutions. Our results indicate that graph reduction and sampling can be effectively combined to address the enumeration bottleneck in maximum compatibility phylogeny, while retaining exact reconstruction when the residual optimum set is completely resolved.   We enhance Cherry's approach to maximum compatibility by introducing graph reduction techniques and quantum sampling. Our classical benchmarks show a clear difference between finding one optimum and recovering the optimum set in practice. We demonstrate the utility of our methods on graphs constructed from SARS-CoV-2 sequences.

papers.title: Can Machine Learning Potentials Be More Accurate Than the Methods They Are Trained On?
papers.abstract: Although machine learning potentials (MLPs) generalize across configurational and chemical compound spaces, their accuracy is commonly believed to be limited by their training methods, with improvements beyond this limit achieved so far only by refitting to experimental observables. In this Perspective, we argue that MLPs can also be made more accurate than their training methods non-empirically by generalizing across a third space, that of quantum-chemical methods. We propose routes to method-transferable MLPs that predict at unseen methods, with working implementations in both density-functional and wavefunction-based theories showing that they can be more accurate than any of their training methods. Aiming beyond the accuracy of the training methods could also make universal MLPs more accurate than single-method models, even when the method-transferable MLPs remain less accurate than those QM methods. Method-transferable MLPs will shape the construction of training datasets and the evaluation of models, pushing the accuracy limits of chemical simulations.

papers.title: Knowledge-Guided Construction of Machine Learning Potentials for Reactive Behavior in Energetic Materials
papers.abstract: Energetic materials involve multiple interactions, making reliable machine-learning potentials (MLPs) difficult to construct without extensive datasets. Here, we enhance the ability of the neural network interatomic potential (NNAP) to describe molecular systems using sphmulti, a refined spherical-harmonic basis set that combines extra radial basis with element-specific chemical weighting in each radial channel. We further integrate hyperactive learning, farthest-point sampling, and iterative sufficiency criteria with knowledge-guided key events, enabling the NNAP to retain essential information for describing the material system. For 3,3'-diamino-4,4'-azoxyfurazan, the resulting NNAP is trained on only 13,680 configurations yet captures key properties, including the isomerization barrier, pyrolysis activation energy, and shock Hugoniot behavior. NNAP-driven molecular dynamics simulations further reveal that pyrolysis proceeds through furazan-ring opening followed by chain reactions, whereas shock loading induces anisotropic hydrogen transfer driven by interlayer structural deformations. This work enables efficient and reliable MLPs for energetic materials.

papers.title: All-electron machine-learned orbital-free density functional for periodic CHNO systems
papers.abstract: We introduce STRUCTURES-P, a machine-learned all-electron orbital-free density functional for periodic CHNO systems. Electrostatics are evaluated analytically in an atom-centered Gaussian basis, while an equivariant network learns the kinetic and exchange-correlation energy from energies and gradients of non-ground-state densities. Minimizing the functional from a superposition of atomic densities recovers the Kohn-Sham ground state: on held-out crystals, the density error falls from 6.7% to 0.4% of the electron count and the energy error reaches 0.25 mHa per atom, half that of a same-architecture interatomic potential. A single functional can be trained for both isolated molecules and periodic systems, and the model generalizes to larger unit cells. It largely preserves relative-energy rankings and reproduces convex-hull vertices on the tested H-N composition slice. Together, these results demonstrate the viability of machine-learned all-electron orbital-free DFT for variational density optimization and energy evaluation in fixed-geometry solids.

papers.title: Mapping Dark Matter in Merging Clusters with Weak Lensing for CSST: Morphology and Filament Recovery
papers.abstract: Weak gravitational lensing offers a direct probe of the projected dark matter distribution in cluster-scale structures and the surrounding cosmic web. We investigate the capability of the China Space Station Telescope (CSST) to recover non-spherical dark matter morphologies using mock reduced-shear maps generated from cosmological N-body simulations. We apply the deep-learning-based MIU2Net mass-reconstruction framework to CSST-like wide- and deep-field source densities, focusing on two representative systems: filament-connected halo pairs and elongated halos. MIU2Net accurately recovers halo centers, elongated mass distributions, and the filamentary structures connecting halo pairs in both survey configurations. Halo centers are localized within about 0.1 h^(-1) Mpc, and elongated-halo shapes and orientations are reliably recovered. Filament paths are stable against shape noise, with mean normalized instability parameters I_F, defined as the mean deviation from the true filament locus in units of R_200, decreasing from 0.041 to 0.037 in the low-redshift bin and from 0.051 to 0.045 in the high-redshift bin from the wide to deep field. The recovered filament shapes remain consistent with the true maps at the percent level. Compared with conventional Kaiser-Squires reconstruction, MIU2Net better preserves low-contrast anisotropic structures while suppressing small-scale noise. These results demonstrate that CSST weak-lensing data, combined with machine-learning-based mass reconstruction, will enable statistical studies of cluster assembly, anisotropic matter accretion, and the connection between massive halos and the filamentary cosmic web.

papers.title: GeoNIRS: Geometry-Aware Pretraining for Heterogeneous fNIRS Representation Learning
papers.abstract: Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) provides portable and spatially localized measurements of cortical hemodynamics, but differences in channel count, probe layout, signal distribution, and task type hinder joint pretraining across datasets. We introduce GeoNIRS, a geometry-aware framework that uses source-detector locations as a shared spatial reference across heterogeneous probe layouts. GeoNIRS compresses variable-size channel sets into a fixed-size latent representation and employs bidirectional HbO/HbR cross-reconstruction with contiguous temporal masking. GeoNIRS-base is pretrained on eight heterogeneous datasets, while GeoNIRS-large scales to 22 datasets. Neither downstream data nor labels are used during pretraining, enabling evaluation under a strict cross-task setting. To our knowledge, GeoNIRS is the first fNIRS framework to explicitly model physical channel geometry during joint pretraining across heterogeneous channel configurations, and the first to provide complete source code and downloadable pretrained checkpoints. We evaluate GeoNIRS on eight held-out tasks spanning clinical and auditory assessment, pain and affective processing, semantic decoding, and motor function. GeoNIRS achieves the highest task-averaged balanced accuracy among the evaluated conventional machine-learning, fNIRS-specific, general time-series, and fNIRS pretraining baselines. Compared with random initialization, pretraining improves average balanced accuracy by 4.12 percentage points under linear probing and 3.30 points under full fine-tuning, with larger benefits when labels are scarce. GeoNIRS also remains robust to missing input channels. Geometry perturbations and pretraining ablations further show that both channel geometry and cross-chromophore reconstruction contribute to the learned representations.

papers.title: Autonomous 3D Visual-Thermal Inspection for Utility-Scale Solar Farms
papers.abstract: Utility-scale photovoltaic (PV) inspection is dominated by aerial surveys, which are effective for identifying module-level hot cells but provide limited visibility of critical components located under the array, including connectors, cabling, fasteners and structural elements. These assets are difficult to inspect consistently at scale, and their defects are often spatially small, partially occluded and difficult to localise from isolated images. We present an automated 3D visual-thermal inspection system (Tricorder) for under-panel PV asset inspection. The approach combines LiDAR-inertial Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) with geometrically calibrated RGB and thermal imagery and machine-learning-based object detection and segmentation. Detected assets are associated with the reconstructed 3D environment, allowing visual and thermal observations from multiple viewpoints to be spatially fused and localised. We demonstrate the approach on utility-scale PV data for MC4 connector detection and connection-state recognition, thermal anomaly identification, and detection of structural components including bolts, nuts and torque tubes. The results demonstrate a pathway from image-based inspection toward spatially grounded autonomous inspection, where defects are detected and linked to specific assets and their 3D locations within the solar farm.

papers.title: PADO-Pauli: A GPU-Accelerated Implementation of Pauli Propagation
papers.abstract: Variational quantum algorithms utilize parameterized circuits many times during training, at new parameter values, over batches of data, and with gradients. Pauli propagation approximates the expectation values of such circuits classically by evolving the observable in the Heisenberg picture as a truncated sum of Pauli strings. We present PADO-Pauli, a GPU engine for Pauli propagation that compiles a circuit and its observables once into sparse matrices in which each rotation angle contributes only a cosine and a sine factor, so every later evaluation reuses the compiled program. It evaluates batches of parameters and data inputs embedded as rotation angles. By default its gradients come from a vector-Jacobian product registered with PyTorch's automatic differentiation, so they flow through the angles to any classical layer that produces them. PADO-Pauli also provides truncation by Pauli weight and coefficient size, and noise channels. Zero-filtering removes terms that do not contribute to an expectation value in the all-zero reference state and makes the batched forward pass about 1.5 times faster. Compared to cuPauliProp on an NVIDIA A100, PADO-Pauli evaluates up to 10 times faster on 4 to 12 qubits and uses up to 3.1 times less memory on 16 qubits. We check its accuracy against exact statevector simulation up to 28 qubits. These features make PADO-Pauli a practical toolkit for training variational quantum algorithms, including quantum machine learning models.

papers.title: DT-LoRA: Reaching Beyond the Tangent Space of Low-Rank Adaptation
papers.abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) often underperforms full fine-tuning. We investigate this performance gap through a tangent-space lens: factorized updates are confined to the tangent space of the current low-rank factors, leaving gradient components outside this space unexploited. An analysis of ten representative LoRA variants reveals that these residual components account for most of the gradient energy and exhibit strong spectral concentration. Motivated by this finding, we propose Dynamic Tangent LoRA (DT-LoRA), which partitions a fixed rank budget into a stable branch and a dynamic branch to capture the principal residual gradient directions. We show that these directions define the optimal update of a local quadratic model under orthogonal-complement and rank constraints. Matrix-free randomized SVD recovers them without materializing the residual gradient, while controlled write-back preserves accumulated updates and stabilizes training within the allocated rank. DT-LoRA adds no trainable parameters or inference cost over LoRA. Experiments across computer vision and natural language processing tasks demonstrate consistent improvements over LoRA and its variants. Moreover, despite being a general-purpose adaptation method, DT-LoRA outperforms task-specific approaches to open-vocabulary domain generalization for semantic segmentation, achieving state-of-the-art results. Code is available at https://github.com/Snipine/DT-LoRA.

papers.title: Representation Geometry and Inductive Biases in Quantum Classifiers across Classical Visual Benchmarks
papers.abstract: Quantum Machine Learning (QML) has a theoretical advantage over classical algorithms for specific synthetic data that is computationally hard. However, it remains unclear whether such theoretical advantages play a meaningful role for realistic classical data, such as natural images. Quantum structural properties induced by unitary operations or entanglement introduce inductive biases that differ from those of classical models, potentially leading to distinct learning behavior on real-world data. In a fully quantum learning pipeline, classical real-world data are first encoded into quantum states via a quantum feature mapping, analogous to a classical feature extractor, and a quantum classifier then classifies the resulting states. Quantum feature mappings generate representations that are difficult to realize classically, while also inducing representation-level biases that do not necessarily match the structure of realistic data. To enable a fair comparison at the classifier level, we focus on the classifier and use classical feature extractors that already provide powerful representations for natural images. By controlling the data scale and supervision strength, we analyze how the unitary structure of quantum classifiers affects generalization, and show that their effectiveness depends strongly on the geometry of the input representations. These results indicate that quantum classifiers benefit from classical features that are aligned with quantum feature spaces. Our analysis shows that kernel alignment identifies representations compatible with quantum feature spaces, providing insights into translating classical models into quantum algorithms.

papers.title: Observation of stacked vortex structure with number controllable Majorana zero mode in Bi$_{2}$Te$_{3}$/FeTe heterojunction
papers.abstract: Creation and control of Majorana zero modes (MZMs) in solid devices is the key challenge in realizing fault tolerant topological quantum computation. Here we report spectroscopic evidence for number controllable MZMs in stoichiometric one quintuple layer Bi$_{2}$Te$_{3}$/FeTe heterostructures, together with the observation of stacked vortices in superconducting islands. Low temperature scanning tunnelling microscopy and spectroscopy reveal a long period moire superlattice arising from lattice mismatch, which induces nanoscale modulation of superconducting gaps. Magnetic vortices exhibit a stacked core structure with two layer derived bound state branches: a dispersive branch evolving into an X-shaped pattern away from the vortex center, and a quantum-limit branch characterized by a spatially unsplit MZMs together with discrete integer quantized Caroli-de Gennes-Matricon states. Notably, MZMs are observed in all measured vortices, and their number can be tuned by magnetic field and the size of Bi$_{2}$Te$_{3}$ islands. These results establish stoichiometric 1QL-Bi$_{2}$Te$_{3}$/FeTe as a patterned superconducting interface that enables isolated and few-vortex Majorana configurations, providing a controlled platform for fuse MZMs.

papers.title: From Syndromes to Computation: A General Framework for Logical Operations in Quantum Error-Correcting Codes
papers.abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computation requires error-correcting codes that not only protect quantum information but also support useful logical operations with practical physical realizations. Here we develop a general framework in which the stabilizer syndromes of commuting Pauli rotations directly organize logical-gate design. We derive an exact codespace-preservation condition valid at arbitrary rotation angles, providing a common stabilizer-level description for CSS and non-CSS codes and for both Clifford and non-Clifford operations. A particularly useful equal-syndrome specialization reduces Clifford gate design to stabilizer factorization, yields a general generator weight bound of $\lceil d/2\rceil$ for distance-$d$ codes, and systematically extends to logical rotations higher in the Clifford hierarchy. Applied to bivariate-bicycle (BB) and non-CSS Mirror qLDPC codes, the framework gives explicit low-weight Clifford and controlled-phase gates. Our implementations yield new low-weight gates, including an addressed $T$ gate on the $[[16,4,4]]$ BB code, $T$-type rotations on the $[[64,8,8]]$ BB code, and CCZ-, CS-, and $T$-type operations on the $[[36,6,6]]$ Mirror code. We also develop analytic constructions using Clifford algebra bases, which turn the syndrome constraints into explicit algebraic relations and provide a systematic route to logical addressability. We use this approach to analytically construct addressed CNOT, SWAP, controlled, and CCZ-type gates on recursive hypercube codes. An independent construction on middle quantum Reed--Muller codes yields C${}^r$Z gates that saturate the equal-syndrome weight bound. These results establish stabilizer syndromes as a constructive link between the stabilizer structure of a quantum code, the logical computations it can directly support, and the fault-tolerance properties of their physical realizations.

papers.title: A grand potential for molten-salt electrochemical phase diagrams from first principles
papers.abstract: The clean-energy transition is driving unprecedented demand for metals, whose extraction is among the largest industrial sources of carbon emissions. Molten-salt electrolysis offers a path toward carbon-free production of aluminum, iron, titanium, and critical metals. However, corrosive operating conditions and complex, multicomponent feedstocks make experimental development costly and challenging. Here, we introduce a first-principles framework for constructing electrochemical phase diagrams of multicomponent systems to accelerate electrode and electrolyte design and guide the selection of compatible materials and operating conditions for electrochemical cells. We derive a grand potential that generates these diagrams at scale, and supply free energies using first-principles data obtained through a fine-tuned foundation machine-learned interatomic potential. For silicon in molten CaCl$_2$, the construction not only recovers the experimental diagram when using the first-principles framework on a limited set of structures, but also predicts further domains when extended to a larger set of crystal structures. Finally, we demonstrate the predictive power of the approach by screening ten alkali and alkaline-earth halide electrolytes for aluminum electrowinning. Three thermodynamic criteria identify NaF, where cryolite emerges as the stable aluminum-bearing phase, recovering the chemistry that Hall and Héroult established empirically in 1886. The framework provides a first-principles basis for selecting compatible electrodes, electrolytes, and operating conditions toward low-carbon metal production from complex source materials.

papers.title: TorchSpin: Differentiable Electron Paramagnetic Resonance Simulation in PyTorch
papers.abstract: Interpreting electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectra commonly requires repeated forward simulation and optimization of spin Hamiltonian parameters. Established software provides mature simulation and fitting methods, but these calculations are not generally available as differentiable components within machine-learning workflows. We present TorchSpin, an open-source PyTorch framework that ports the organization and numerical conventions of EasySpin into a tensor-based computational environment. Representative calculations spanning continuous-wave EPR, ENDOR, pulse EPR, spin dynamics, trajectory simulation, and magnetometry closely reproduced corresponding EasySpin results. In matched benchmarks, TorchSpin CPU execution was faster than EasySpin for six of nine workloads although performance depended strongly on the calculation. We therefore focused on the capabilities enabled by automatic differentiation in PyTorch. In a Cu(II) powder-spectrum demonstration, feedback propagated through TorchSpin improved the quality of a supervised convolutional neural network (CNN) without using parameter labels during refinement. Models trained from randomly initialized CNNs using only noisy spectra and TorchSpin reconstruction loss achieved median similarities of $\geq$ 0.99. CNNs trained on TorchSpin-generated libraries also transferred without adaptation to independently generated EasySpin spectra with performance comparable to EasySpin-trained controls. Once trained, the CNN produced initial parameter estimates in approximately 1 ms per spectrum while a batch of 512 was processed in approximately 1.3 ms with GPU acceleration. TorchSpin therefore provides both a tested Python implementation of established EPR calculations and a differentiable physical layer for rapid learned inference, spectral refinement, and parameter-label-free training.

papers.title: Structure-preserving fidelity diagnostics for partial differential equations
papers.abstract: Machine learning surrogates of partial differential equations (PDEs) are commonly trained on data generated by numerical solvers. Therefore, the training data obey not the PDE but the modified equation of the numerical scheme, and the test loss, computed on data from the same solver, cannot distinguish a model that learned the physics from one that learned the discretization error. Here, we show that the difference is nevertheless visible in the trained model. We propose a suite of structure-preserving fidelity diagnostics, simple scores that measure whether a learned model respects one known property of the physics, such as a conserved quantity, a symmetry or a Hamiltonian structure, without access to the training data or the governing equation. Over five systems, the diagnostics track the error with respect to the true dynamics with a rank correlation of up to $0.94$, while the test loss is uncorrelated or anti-correlated with it. For the Burgers, Korteweg-de Vries and Navier-Stokes equations, the diagnostics separate numerical schemes that the test loss ranks as equivalent, including schemes of the same order. order.

papers.title: Time-Domain Observables for Resonant Scattering in Quantum Simulations of Lattice Gauge Theory
papers.abstract: Quantum computing may allow unprecedented access to nonequilibrium quantum dynamics, including problems of interest in particle physics, like the real-time development of scattering processes. Although fault-tolerant simulations at scale are still in the future, recent advancements toward early fault-tolerant simulations motivate building increasingly elaborate benchmark problems in order to assess state-of-the-art capabilities and test new algorithms and observables. In this work, we study glueball scattering on a line-of-plaquettes lattice in pure $SU(3)$ lattice gauge theory. We characterize scattering of the lowest-energy glueball states using classical exact diagonalization methods, identifying the continuum resonance structure using real-time simulations and approximate analytic methods, and we propose time-domain observables for extracting properties of the resonance from quantum simulations. We furthermore construct a toy model that shares the spectral features of the lattice gauge theory and demonstrate extraction of the observables. Feasibility on near-term hardware is demonstrated through simulation of a resonant collision of this toy model on Quantinuum System Model $\texttt{H2-2}$, with a 14-plaquette chain encoded in 28 qubits. The Trotterized circuit after optimization and compression requires $\sim 25n$ entangling gates for $n$ Trotter steps.

papers.title: Assessing the Performance of AI Models in Misinformation Detection Using Predefined Social Noise Constructs
papers.abstract: Social media platforms generate vast volumes of user-generated content that often obscure meaningful discourse, a phenomenon conceptualized as social noise. While existing misinformation detection methods primarily focus on factual verification, they largely overlook the role of social noise in amplifying misinformation. This study assesses the performance of six text-based models and a graph neural network (GNN) in mitigating the effects of misinformation using predefined social noise constructs. The dataset consists of 500,000 tweets collected from the X platform using the Ukraine hashtag during the Russia-Ukraine conflict from March 2024 to March 2025. Advanced machine learning models achieve strong performance, with accuracies ranging from 79.94% to 97.17%. RoBERTa demonstrates the highest performance, with an accuracy of 97.17%, Cohen's kappa of 0.9660, MCC of 0.9660, and AUC of 0.9977. The GNN achieves an accuracy of 64.52% and an AUC of 0.899, demonstrating performance above random-chance classification by exploiting the relational structure between tweets. All text-based models achieve kappa values greater than 0.75, indicating substantial overall agreement. Explainable AI analysis using LIME reveals that 89.6% of predictive weight is attributed to contextual features rather than isolated keywords. The findings highlight that integrating social noise into AI pipelines enhances misinformation detection and supports more effective mitigation strategies in large-scale social media environments.

papers.title: Agency as a New Organizing Abstraction for Computer Science
papers.abstract: Advances in large-scale machine learning have enabled agentic AI systems: persistent, autonomous computational entities that pursue goals, initiate actions, and interact with open environments. These systems are often framed as applications of foundation models. We argue that this framing is incomplete: agency is also a candidate new organizing abstraction for computer science. What is new is not the concept of an agent, nor runtime policy generation per se, but its general-purpose, open-ended form, in which systems can synthesize courses of action from goals, observations, and memory, over tools and environments for which no complete task-specific model was specified in advance. Thus agency becomes a systems-level abstraction as well as an AI modeling concept. Where the process abstraction organizes computation around executing programs, agency organizes it around pursuing goals under bounded resources: a process executes a program; an agent pursues a goal. From this perspective, the recurring failures of deployed agentic systems (runaway resource consumption, behavior redirected by adversarial content, opaque continuous operation) are symptoms of structural abstraction gaps, not isolated engineering defects. We examine these gaps across six dimensions (execution, interfaces, correctness, oversight, coordination, and persistence) and argue that closing them requires coordinated advances in systems,

papers.title: Event-Centric Earthquake Monitoring with a Multi-Station Transformer
papers.abstract: Earthquake catalogs underpin studies such as fault structure, earthquake processes and seismic hazard, and their value depends on being both complete and reliable. Machine learning has improved individual tasks of earthquake monitoring, but processing stations independently discards the consistency of arrivals across the network, and running tasks in sequence fragments the information describing each earthquake. We present EQNet2, a geometry-aware multi-station Transformer that jointly predicts phase arrivals, first-motion polarities, source location and magnitude, and the association of arrivals into events. On a Northern California test dataset and on continuous waveforms from Ridgecrest and the San Francisco Bay Area, EQNet2 recovers more weak arrivals, produces fewer false detections, and associates more picks into located events. Its learned attention links information across stations along time--distance patterns consistent with seismic moveout. As seismic networks grow denser, exploiting multi-station coherence and event-centric prediction offers a path to more complete and reliable catalogs.

papers.title: A Method for Exact Enforcement of Boundary Conditions on General Curved Triangular Domains: Algorithm and Application to Scientific Machine Learning
papers.abstract: We present a method for enforcing exactly Dirichlet, Neumann, and Robin conditions on general triangular domains with arbitrarily curved boundaries. The algorithmic constructions developed here complements those in a previous work for general quadrilateral domains. Our method combines (i) the exact mapping between a general curved triangular domain and the standard triangle, (ii) TFC constrained expressions, and (iii) Barnhill transfinite interpolations, to provide explicit closed-form trial ansatze that mathematically satisfy the imposed boundary conditions exactly. Corner compatibility induced by the boundary conditions is pivotal, and enforcing exactly the imposed boundary conditions hinges on the exact enforcement of the induced compatibility constraints. The corner compatibility associated with the acute vertices of the standard triangle and the coupling between gradient components when the hypotenuse corresponds to a Neumann/Robin boundary pose particular challenges. Two strategies are critical to resolving these issues, by reformulating conditional corner constraints into equivalent unconditional forms and by introducing a separate TFC-style auxiliary edge construction together with an associated linear solve on the hypotenuse. We analyze the corner compatibility constraints and present formulations for the general form of functions that exactly satisfy the imposed Dirichlet, Neumann, or Robin conditions on curved triangular domains. The proposed method has been implemented using extreme learning machine type randomized neural networks for solving PDE problems. We present ample numerical experiments with linear/nonlinear PDE problems on a variety of domains with complex boundary geometries. Numerical results show that the current method has enforced the Dirichlet, Neumann, and Robin conditions on curved domain boundaries to the machine precision.

papers.title: Learning to Play: Reinforcement Learning and Games
papers.abstract: Amazing breakthroughs in reinforcement learning have taken place. Computers teach themselves to play Chess and Go and beat world champions. There is talk about expanding application areas towards general artificial intelligence (AI). The breakthroughs in Backgammon, Checkers, Chess, Atari, Go, Poker, and StarCraft have shown that we can build machines that exhibit intelligent game playing of the highest level. These successes have been widely publicized in the media, and inspire AI entrepreneurs and scientists alike. Reinforcement learning in games has become a mainstream AI research topic. It is a broad topic, and the successes build on a range of diverse techniques, from exact planning algorithms, to adaptive sampling, deep function approximation, and ingenious self-play methods. Perhaps because of the breadth of these technologies, or because of the recency of the breakthroughs, there are few books that explain these methods in depth. This book covers all methods in one comprehensive volume, explaining the latest research, bringing you as close as possible to working implementations, with many references to the original research papers. The programming examples in this book are in Python, the language in which most current reinforcement learning research is conducted. We help you to get started with machine learning frameworks such as Gym, TensorFlow, and Keras, and provide exercises to help understand how AI is learning to play.

papers.title: Measure Neural Mappings
papers.abstract: We introduce and define measure neural mappings (MNMs), which combine measure-dependent neural transport with ensemble consistency for learning operators on probability measures. Ensemble consistency requires outputs from growing ensembles sampled from an input law to converge to the specified population output in probability. We establish quantitative continuum limits for attention on noncompact laws under strong sub-Gaussian and tail-integrability assumptions. These laws accommodate unbounded state spaces in scientific machine learning, including Bayesian inference and uncertainty quantification. For fixed self-attention transformers, the expected output Wasserstein error is bounded by the empirical input Wasserstein error plus an additional $N^{-1/2}$ attention term. These self-attention transformers are MNMs under the stated assumptions: pre-norm architectures follow from compact stability after normalization, while post-norm architectures are covered under the stated tail conditions. We prove corresponding cross-attention estimates and extend the results to multihead attention and grouped transformer evaluation, with convergence as the group size grows. For Set Transformers viewed as measure-to-vector mappings, we obtain an $N^{-1/2}$ bound on the expected Euclidean output error under the stated assumptions. Experiments on seven operators in dimensions $d=1,2,3,5,10$ support the predicted particle-count dependence, using one-dimensional Wasserstein computations and Sinkhorn approximations in higher dimensions. The observed Wasserstein and sliced Wasserstein decay rates are close to their respective theoretical sampling benchmarks.

papers.title: Mitigating Black-Box Score-Based Query Attacks via Gradient Confusion
papers.abstract: Score-based black-box adversarial attacks pose a serious threat to deployed machine learning systems by exploiting repeated model queries to craft adversarial examples, requiring neither access to model parameters nor architecture. Existing defenses predominantly rely on stochastic output perturbations, which fail to prevent determined attackers from recovering stable gradient estimates by increasing query budgets or averaging over randomness. In this work, we propose the Gradient Confusion Defense (GCD), a retraining-free, deterministic test-time wrapper that actively shapes the probability vector returned to querying adversaries. By solving a constrained optimization problem grounded in the model's Jacobian, GCD aligns the exposed logit-gradient with a target confusion direction that is maximally misaligned with the true adversarial loss gradient---increasing the query complexity of attacks without sacrificing predictive utility or top-1 accuracy. We provide rigorous theoretical analysis demonstrating that GCD provably slows gradient-estimation-based attacks and induces systematic accept/reject errors in random search-based attacks, with the confusion effect amplifying as the fraction of defended queries increases. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet across multiple architectures (ResNet-18, ResNet-50, ViT-B/16) and four state-of-the-art attacks confirm these predictions: GCD achieves state-of-the-art robustness, while incurring zero clean accuracy degradation. %Crucially, unlike randomization-based defenses, GCD's deterministic structure provides resilience against adaptive attacks that exploit stochasticity, making it well-suited for security-critical deployment settings.

papers.title: Wisevolve Potential Engine: Machine-Learning Molecular Dynamics at 100 Million Atom-Steps per Second on a Single GPU
papers.abstract: General-purpose molecular dynamics software supports diverse interatomic potentials and simulation requirements. Within a simulation stage, the loaded potential model and the required calculations typically remain fixed as the atomic configuration evolves. We present the Wisevolve Potential Engine (WPE), which uses this information from GPUMD to select and reuse a GPU execution policy tailored to the model and simulation stage. GPUMD retains simulation control and ownership of the simulation data. On a single NVIDIA RTX 5090, WPE-enabled GPUMD (GPUMD-WPE) achieves a median throughput of 109 million atom-step/s across 106 neuroevolution potential (NEP) workloads. For a 15.1-million-atom diamond Si system, it sustains 142 million atom-step/s. Relative to GPUMD, geometric-mean speedups are 3.49x across these NEP workloads, 3.61x across 16 workloads using NEP with dynamic charges (qNEP), 1.24x across 28 classical-potential workloads, and 10.5x across 56 path-integral molecular dynamics (PIMD) configurations. End-to-end calculations of water structure, lattice thermal conductivity, and PIMD thermal expansion show close agreement with corresponding GPUMD results and published simulation results. A separate 12.5-million-atom Cu shock-compression simulation demonstrates its applicability to large-scale nonequilibrium dynamics. These results support model- and stage-specific specialization as a practical way to accelerate GPU potential evaluation in general-purpose molecular dynamics workflows.

papers.title: Collision Cascade Morphology and Defect Nucleation in Pure Tungsten and an Equimolar Refractory W-Ta-Cr-V Alloy
papers.abstract: Collision cascades and defect-formation mechanisms in pure W and the WTaCrV refractory high-entropy alloy were investigated using molecular dynamics simulations over primary knock-on atom (PKA) energies of 0.1-100 keV. Machine-learning tabulated Gaussian approximation potentials (tabGAP), complemented by short-range Ziegler-Biersack-Littmark (ZBL) interactions, were employed. Analysis of the heat spike lifetime, affected region, atomic relocations and surviving defects reveals an importance of subcascade formation and presence of light elements in the alloy. Cascade splitting into subcascades contributes to the distribution of the PKA energy over a larger region in the material, nucleating less dislocations and smaller voids - latter being present only in W and absent in WTaCrV. Since cascade splitting is more frequently observed in WTaCrV, the alloy shows better resistance to primary irradiation damage compared to pure W. Apart from cascade splitting, analysis of interstitials shows that Cr and to lesser extent V, being lighter and smaller elements, accommodate the damage in form of point defects, contributing to the mitigation of formation of the dislocation loops.

papers.title: Can Universal Machine-Learning Interatomic Potentials Capture Small Polarons? A Geometry-Based Benchmark in Transition-Metal Oxides
papers.abstract: Small polarons, formed when excess electrons become localized through lattice distortions, play a critical role in charge transport, catalysis, and degradation processes in transition-metal (TM) oxides. Whether universal machine-learning interatomic potentials (uMLIPs), which lack explicit electronic degrees of freedom, can describe them remains unclear. Here, we investigate H-induced electron localization across a range of TM oxides using a geometric descriptor based on TM-O bond-length expansion (Z-score) to identify polaronic distortions. We find that uMLIPs exhibit varying degrees of electron localization, from delocalized states to metastable small polarons, with their behavior strongly dependent on the training data and treatment of electronic correlations. In particular, the absence of Hubbard U corrections for specific TM cations in the training data leads to electron delocalization, in contrast to DFT+U predictions. Although some uMLIPs reproduce polaron hopping barriers during coupled proton-polaron transfer, all of them fail to stabilize spatially separated polaron-donor configurations, instead favoring localization near the H dopant.

papers.title: Machine-learned topological transport of magnetic colloids
papers.abstract: By modulating the orientation of a uniform magnetic field it is possible to transport magnetic microparticles above magnetic patterns. In periodic patterns, driving control loops that wind around special orientations, which are dictated by the symmetry of the pattern, induce transport by one unit cell. The transport is topologically protected with trajectories controlled by the winding numbers of the control loop around the special orientations. In non-periodic patterns, the special orientations are position dependent, precluding a global characterization of the transport using a small set of winding numbers. We use here a reinforcement learning agent trained with Brownian dynamics simulation data that uses the local environment of the magnetic pattern to decide an action over the control loop. The agent autonomously discovers topological transport protocols directly from the particle response without prior characterization of the magnetic potential landscape. An agent trained solely on a complex non-periodic pattern directly generalizes to completely unseen periodic, quasicrystalline, and disordered substrates. Moreover, the agent dynamically adjusts the control loop to transport particles across lattice defects and to counterbalance external drift forces that would cause static topological loops to fail. By adding a pathfinding algorithm to the model, we additionally achieve simultaneous, independent transport of multiple identical colloids along different on demand trajectories. We demonstrate that the control loops can be directly transferred to an experimental setup to successfully drive magnetic microparticles across a non-uniform magnetic thin film.
